stem: A file has permission mode 644 (rw-r--r--). What can users in the file's group do?

options.text: Read only
Read and write
Read, write, and execute
Nothing

explanation: 644 breaks down as owner=rw(6), group=r(4), others=r(4). The group digit 4 grants read only.

stem: Which command prints the full path of your current working directory?

options.text: pwd
ls
cd
mkdir

explanation: pwd (print working directory) outputs the absolute path of the shell's current directory.

stem: A file has mode 640. Who can read it?

options.text: Owner only
Owner and group
Everyone
Group only

explanation: 6 = rw for owner, 4 = r for group, 0 = nothing for others. So owner and group can read.

stem: You are in /home/user/projects. Which command takes you to /home/user?

options.text: cd ..
cd .
cd /
cd ~/projects

explanation: '..' refers to the parent directory, so 'cd ..' moves up one level from /home/user/projects to /home/user.

stem: You want to ask process 4521 to shut down gracefully (not kill it forcefully). Which command does this?

options.text: kill -9 4521
kill 4521
kill -STOP 4521
killall -u 4521

explanation: 'kill' with no signal flag sends SIGTERM (15), a graceful shutdown request. -9 sends SIGKILL (forceful, unignorable); -STOP suspends the process without ending it; killall -u filters by username, not PID.

stem: Which command prints only the PIDs of all running processes named 'nginx'?

options.text: pgrep nginx
ps nginx
grep nginx
top nginx

explanation: pgrep matches processes by name and prints their PIDs. 'ps nginx' is not valid usage, 'grep nginx' needs piped input, and 'top' doesn't take a process name argument this way.

stem: In bash, which syntax reads the value of a variable named NAME?

options.text: $NAME
%NAME
&NAME
#NAME

explanation: The $ prefix expands a bash variable's value. The other symbols have different meanings (job control, backgrounding, comments).

stem: Which keyword starts a bash loop that iterates once per item in a list, e.g. `for x in a b c; do ...; done`?

options.text: for
if
case
until

explanation: 'for VAR in LIST; do ...; done' iterates VAR over each item in LIST. 'if' and 'case' are conditionals, not loops; 'until' loops on a condition, not a list.

stem:
What does this print?
NAME=World
echo "Hello $NAME"

options.text: Hello $NAME
Hello World
Hello
Error: NAME not defined

explanation: Double quotes allow variable expansion, so $NAME is replaced with its value 'World' before printing.

stem: Which command prints only the lines containing the word 'error' from file.log?

options.text: grep error file.log
sed error file.log
awk error file.log
cut error file.log

explanation: grep searches for a pattern and prints matching lines. sed and awk need a script/program argument, not a bare word, to filter this way; cut extracts columns, not pattern matches.

stem: What does `set -e` do at the top of a bash script?

options.text: Enables debug tracing of each command before it runs
Exits the script immediately if any command returns a non-zero status
Suppresses all error messages
Enables extended globbing patterns

explanation: 'set -e' makes the script stop at the first command that fails, instead of continuing with later commands. Debug tracing is 'set -x'; it doesn't suppress messages or affect globbing.

stem: Which command replaces only the FIRST occurrence of 'foo' with 'bar' on each line of file.txt, printing the result to stdout?

options.text: sed 's/foo/bar/' file.txt
sed 's/foo/bar/g' file.txt
sed -n 's/foo/bar/' file.txt
sed '/foo/bar/' file.txt

explanation: Without the 'g' flag, sed's s/// command replaces only the first match per line. The 'g' flag (option b) replaces every match; '-n' (option c) suppresses automatic printing so nothing would print; option d is not valid sed syntax for substitution.

stem: Which built-in function opens a file for reading in Python?

options.text: open()
read()
load()
file()

explanation: open() returns a file object; .read() is then called on that object. load() and file() are not the standard way to open files in current Python.

stem: Which block is used to catch an exception in Python?

options.text: except
catch
rescue
handle

explanation: Python uses try/except to catch exceptions. 'catch' and 'rescue' are keywords from other languages (Java/JS, Ruby); 'handle' is not a Python keyword.

stem: Which standard library module provides os.path.join() and os.listdir() for working with the filesystem?

options.text: os
sys
re
json

explanation: The os module wraps operating-system filesystem operations. sys exposes interpreter state, re is for regular expressions, and json is for JSON encoding/decoding.

stem: Which function runs a shell command, waits for it to finish, and returns a CompletedProcess object?

options.text: subprocess.run()
subprocess.Popen()
os.system()
subprocess.call()

explanation: subprocess.run() is the modern, recommended API: it blocks until the command finishes and returns a CompletedProcess with output, return code, etc. Popen is lower-level and doesn't wait by itself; os.system() and subprocess.call() only return an integer exit code.

options.text: A then C
B then C
A then B then C
C only

explanation: The division raises ZeroDivisionError, so 'A' prints from the except block. 'else' only runs if NO exception occurred, so 'B' is skipped. 'finally' always runs, so 'C' prints last.

stem: Given `result = subprocess.run(['ls', '-l'], capture_output=True, text=True)`, how do you access the command's standard output as a string?

options.text: result.stdout
result.output
result.stdout.decode()
result.out

explanation: With text=True, result.stdout is already a decoded str, so .decode() would fail (option c assumes bytes). CompletedProcess has no .output or .out attribute.

stem: Which command stages all changes in the current directory for the next commit?

options.text: git add .
git commit .
git push .
git stage --all

explanation: 'git add .' stages every changed file under the current directory. commit and push operate on already-staged/committed changes; 'git stage --all' is not a standard git command.

stem: Which command creates a new branch named 'feature-x' and switches to it in one step?

options.text: git checkout -b feature-x
git branch feature-x
git merge feature-x
git switch feature-x

explanation: 'checkout -b' creates the branch and switches to it immediately. 'git branch' alone only creates it without switching; 'git switch feature-x' without -c would fail since the branch doesn't exist yet.

stem: You ran `git commit -m 'fix bug'` but forgot to stage a changed file. After staging that file with `git add`, which command adds it into the previous commit instead of creating a new one?

options.text: git commit --amend
git commit --fixup
git rebase -i
git cherry-pick

explanation: 'git commit --amend' replaces the most recent commit with a new one that includes the currently staged changes. The other commands either prepare a separate fixup commit or operate on commit history/ranges, not the immediately preceding commit.

stem: Which command downloads commits from a remote repository WITHOUT merging them into your current branch?

options.text: git fetch
git pull
git clone
git push

explanation: git fetch updates your local copy of the remote's branches without touching your working branch. git pull is fetch followed by merge; clone is for an initial copy, not ongoing sync; push sends commits, it doesn't download them.

stem: During a merge, git reports a conflict in file.txt. After manually editing the file to resolve the conflict, what are the next two steps?

options.text: git add file.txt, then git commit
git checkout file.txt, then git push
git reset file.txt, then git merge --continue
git stash, then git merge --abort

explanation: After hand-resolving a conflict, staging the file with 'git add' marks it resolved, and 'git commit' completes the merge. 'git checkout file.txt' would discard your edits; 'reset' unstages rather than resolves; 'merge --abort' cancels the merge entirely.

stem: What does `git push --force` risk that `git push --force-with-lease` protects against?

options.text: Overwriting remote commits that someone else pushed since your last fetch
Losing your own local uncommitted changes in the working tree
Deleting the remote branch entirely along with its history
Corrupting the local .git directory and its object store

explanation: '--force-with-lease' checks that the remote branch still points where you last saw it before overwriting, so it refuses the push if someone else has pushed in the meantime. Plain '--force' overwrites blindly, which can silently discard a teammate's commits.

stem: Which protocol provides reliable, ordered delivery of data between two hosts?

options.text: TCP
UDP
ICMP
ARP

explanation: TCP numbers segments, acknowledges them and retransmits lost ones. UDP is connectionless and does none of this.

stem: Which default port does HTTPS use?
explanation: HTTPS listens on 443 by default. 80 is plain HTTP and 22 is SSH.

stem: Which DNS record type maps a hostname to an IPv4 address?

options.text: MX record
TXT record
A record
NS record

explanation: An A record holds an IPv4 address. AAAA is the IPv6 version, MX names mail servers and NS names name servers.

stem: A firewall allows inbound TCP 22 only from 10.0.0.0/24. A host at 10.0.1.5 tries to SSH in. What happens?

options.text: The connection is allowed because port 22 is open to every address
The connection is allowed because SSH ignores any firewall source address rules
The connection is blocked because SSH must use port 443 instead
The connection is blocked because its address is outside the allowed range

explanation: 10.0.0.0/24 covers 10.0.0.0 to 10.0.0.255, so 10.0.1.5 does not match the rule and the default deny applies.

stem: Which sequence correctly describes how a TCP connection is set up?

options.text: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK
SYN, ACK, SYN-ACK
ACK, SYN, SYN-ACK
SYN-ACK, SYN, ACK

explanation: The client sends SYN, the server answers SYN-ACK and the client completes with ACK: the three-way handshake.

stem: A DNS record has a TTL of 3600 seconds and you change its IP. Why might some users still reach the old IP for up to an hour?

options.text: Browsers refuse any new IP address until the whole computer is restarted
Resolvers may keep serving the cached answer until the TTL expires
Authoritative name servers reject all record changes within the first hour
HTTP/1.1 pins the old IP address until a new TLS handshake is performed

explanation: Resolvers cache answers for the TTL. Lowering the TTL before a planned change shortens this window.

stem: In a typical CI pipeline, which stage normally runs first?

options.text: Build and compile the code
Deploy the release to production
Promote the artifact to the live registry
Send the release announcement email

explanation: Later stages need something to test and package, so the pipeline starts by building the code.

stem: Which event commonly triggers a CI build automatically?

options.text: A change to the team's chat channel topic
A commit pushed to the repository
A server disk reaching fifty percent usage
A new member joining the organisation

explanation: CI systems listen for pushes and pull requests through webhooks and start a build on each.

stem: What does "build once, promote the same artifact" mean?

options.text: Each environment compiles its own fresh build from the source code
Production builds are rebuilt with extra optimisation flags switched on
The exact artifact tested in staging is the one deployed to production
Only the final environment stores a build artifact for later use

explanation: Rebuilding per environment can produce a different binary. Promoting one artifact means what you tested is what you ship.

stem: A pipeline has the stages build, unit test, integration test and deploy. The unit test stage fails. What should happen by default?

options.text: The deploy stage still runs, since the build itself succeeded
The pipeline retries the build stage until the tests finally pass
The failed tests are ignored and logged as warnings only
Later stages are skipped and the pipeline is marked failed

explanation: Stages run in order and a failure stops the pipeline, which stops broken code from reaching deployment.

stem: A monorepo pipeline rebuilds every service on any commit and takes 40 minutes. Which change reduces build time most safely?

options.text: Path-based triggers that build only the services whose files changed
Skip the tests for every service except the one deployed last
Turn off all caching so every build always starts from a clean workspace
Merge all services into one image so they are built together

explanation: Path filters keep the safety of testing what changed and avoid rebuilding what did not.

stem: Why are artifacts tagged with an immutable version such as a commit SHA instead of only latest?

options.text: Registries refuse to store images that are tagged with the name latest
Any deployment can be traced to exact code, reproduced or rolled back
Latest tags make images slower to pull from registries than other tags
Old versions are deleted automatically after each new deployment

explanation: latest moves, so it cannot tell you what is running. A fixed tag ties a deployment to one build.

stem: Which Dockerfile instruction sets the base image?

options.text: RUN
CMD
FROM
COPY

explanation: FROM names the image the new image builds on. RUN executes a command at build time, CMD sets the default start command.

stem: What is a Docker image?

options.text: A running instance of an application and its process tree
A virtual machine that has its own kernel
A network bridge between several containers
A read-only template used to create containers

explanation: An image is the packaged filesystem and metadata. A container is a running instance created from it.

stem: A container writes database files to its own filesystem and the data is lost when the container is removed. What prevents this?

options.text: Mounting a volume at the database's data directory
Publishing the database port with the -p flag
Giving the container more memory with the --memory flag
Using the host network mode for the container

explanation: A container's writable layer is deleted with it. A volume lives outside the container and survives removal.

stem: A Dockerfile copies the source code first and then runs npm install. Why does this slow rebuilds?

options.text: Docker never caches layers created by a RUN instruction that uses a package manager
Any source change invalidates the layer cache, so dependencies reinstall every time
npm install always needs a fresh network connection on each separate build
COPY instructions are executed when the container starts rather than at build time

explanation: Layers are cached in order. Copy package files first and install, then copy the rest, so the install layer is reused.

stem: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?

options.text: CMD runs during the image build and ENTRYPOINT runs only when the container starts
ENTRYPOINT can only launch shell scripts while CMD can only launch compiled binaries
ENTRYPOINT sets the main executable while CMD supplies default arguments that can be overridden
They are aliases and Docker keeps whichever one appears last in the Dockerfile

explanation: ENTRYPOINT defines what runs. CMD gives default arguments, which docker run can replace.

stem: Two containers on the default bridge network cannot reach each other by container name. What is the usual fix?

options.text: Expose both containers' ports with the -P flag on the host
Run both containers with the --privileged flag switched on
Set the same hostname inside every one of the containers
Attach both to a user-defined bridge network, which provides name resolution

explanation: The default bridge does not resolve names. User-defined bridge networks include built-in DNS.

stem: Which kind of cloud storage suits images and backups stored as objects?

options.text: Block storage attached to one VM
An in-memory cache cluster
A relational database server
Object storage such as S3

explanation: Object storage holds files as objects behind an HTTP API, scales well and suits images and backups.

stem: What is the principle of least privilege?

options.text: Give each identity only the permissions it needs
Grant all engineers the same broad administrator role
Let identities choose their own permissions on demand
Remove all permissions from service accounts entirely

explanation: Limiting permissions limits the damage from a mistake or a stolen credential.

stem: Which design survives the failure of a whole availability zone?

options.text: Run several larger instances inside a single availability zone
Run instances across two or more availability zones behind a load balancer
Take nightly snapshots of one instance in one zone
Use a bigger instance type with more CPU and memory

explanation: A zone is a failure domain. Spreading instances across zones lets the service keep running when one fails.

stem: An instance in a private subnet must download updates from the internet without being reachable from it. What is typically used?

options.text: An internet gateway attached directly to its private subnet
A public IP address assigned straight to the instance
A NAT gateway placed in a public subnet with a route from the private one
A VPN tunnel set up between the instance and the registry

explanation: A NAT gateway lets private instances start outbound connections while blocking inbound ones.

stem: An application on a VM needs to read one storage bucket. Which approach is safest?

options.text: Store an administrator access key in the application's config file
Make the bucket public so no credentials are needed at all
Share one engineer's personal access key through the team chat
Attach a role with read-only access to that bucket to the VM

explanation: A role gives short-lived credentials with narrow permissions and no secret to leak or rotate by hand.

stem: What does a Recovery Time Objective (RTO) of 15 minutes mean?

options.text: The service should be restored within 15 minutes of an outage
No more than 15 minutes of data may be lost in an outage
Backups must be taken every 15 minutes without exception
Each deployment must finish within 15 minutes of the build starting

explanation: RTO is about time to recover. The amount of data you can afford to lose is the Recovery Point Objective (RPO).

stem: What is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes?

options.text: A node
A pod
A namespace
A cluster

explanation: A pod wraps one or more containers that share networking and storage. It is what the scheduler places on a node.

stem: What gives a set of pods a stable network address?

options.text: A ConfigMap
A PersistentVolume
A Service
A Namespace

explanation: Pods come and go with changing IPs. A Service gives them one stable address and balances across them.

stem: You change the image tag in a Deployment. What happens by default?

options.text: All pods are deleted at once and then recreated
Nothing changes until each node is restarted by hand
Only newly scheduled pods use the new image tag
Pods are replaced gradually in a rolling update

explanation: The default strategy starts new pods and removes old ones in steps, so the app stays available.

stem: What does a failing readiness probe do?

options.text: The pod is removed from Service endpoints but is not restarted
The pod is restarted immediately by the kubelet
The node is drained and marked unschedulable
The Deployment is rolled back automatically to its previous revision

explanation: Readiness controls whether traffic is sent to the pod. A failing liveness probe is what triggers a restart.

stem: Which resource routes HTTP traffic by host name and path to different Services?

options.text: A ClusterIP Service on its own
An Ingress, served by an ingress controller
A NodePort Service on every node
A headless Service with no selector and no cluster IP

explanation: Ingress rules describe host and path routing, and an ingress controller turns them into a working proxy.

stem: A Horizontal Pod Autoscaler targets 50% CPU. Two replicas average 100% CPU. About how many replicas will it aim for?

options.text: About 3 replicas
About 2 replicas
About 4 replicas
About 8 replicas

explanation: Desired replicas = current replicas x (current metric / target) = 2 x (100 / 50) = 4.

stem: Which Terraform command previews changes without applying them?

options.text: terraform apply
terraform init
terraform plan
terraform destroy

explanation: plan compares the configuration and state with real infrastructure and shows what would change.

stem: What is a Terraform module?

options.text: A plugin that talks to a cloud provider's API
A file that stores the current state of resources
A command that formats the configuration files
A reusable group of resources defined together

explanation: Modules package related resources with inputs and outputs so they can be reused.

stem: Why store Terraform state in a remote backend with locking?

options.text: A team shares one state and two applies cannot run at once
Terraform can then run without any provider plugins installed
State files are never needed again after the first apply
Resources are created faster in parallel across many runs

explanation: Local state breaks teamwork. A remote backend shares it and locking prevents conflicting writes.

stem: You rename a resource block but keep the same real infrastructure. What does plan show by default?

options.text: No changes, because the real infrastructure is unchanged
Destroy the resource under the old name and create one under the new name
An error because resource names cannot be changed
Only an update to the tags of the existing resource

explanation: State tracks resources by address. A new address looks like a new resource unless you add a moved block.

stem: Someone changes a security group in the cloud console by hand. What does the next terraform plan show?

options.text: No difference at all, since Terraform ignores changes made outside of it
An error telling you to delete the state file first
A diff that reverts the manual change to match the configuration
A diff that copies the console change into the code

explanation: Terraform refreshes real state and plans to bring it back to the configuration. This is configuration drift.

stem: A variable is marked sensitive = true. What does that do?

options.text: It encrypts the value inside the state file with a project key
It prevents the variable from being passed to any module
It deletes the value from state after the apply completes
It hides the value in plan and apply output, but it is still stored in state

explanation: sensitive only redacts output. State can still contain the value, so protect the state backend.

stem: What does idempotent mean for a configuration task?

options.text: It runs only once and then disables itself
Running it repeatedly gives the same end state
It always restarts the service it manages
It runs in parallel on every server in the inventory at once

explanation: An idempotent task changes something only if it is not already in the desired state.

stem: In Ansible, what does the inventory define?

options.text: The tasks that are executed on each host
The variable files that hold all of the project's secrets
The hosts and groups that playbooks run against
The modules that are installed locally

explanation: The inventory lists the machines and how they are grouped. Playbooks list what to do on them.

stem: Which task is idempotent?

options.text: A command that appends a line to a config file on every run
A script that creates a new numbered backup on each run
A shell task that increments a counter stored in a file
The package module with state set to present for nginx

explanation: The package module checks whether nginx is installed and acts only if it is not.

stem: Where should database passwords used by playbooks be stored?

options.text: In an encrypted vault or secret manager, not as plain text in the repository
In a plain variables file committed with the playbooks
In the inventory file next to the host names
In a comment above the task that needs them

explanation: Secrets in Git are exposed to everyone with access and stay in history. Use Ansible Vault or a secret manager.

stem: What is the benefit of a dynamic inventory in a cloud environment?

options.text: Playbooks run faster because fewer modules need to be loaded each time
Hosts are discovered from the cloud API, so the list stays current as servers change
Variables no longer need to be defined for each group of hosts
SSH keys are generated automatically for every newly created host

explanation: Servers appear and disappear in the cloud, so a hand-edited list goes stale. A dynamic inventory asks the provider.

stem: A handler is notified by two tasks on the same host in one play. How many times does it run on that host?

options.text: Twice, once after each notifying task
Never, because handlers only run when called by name
Once, after the tasks in the play finish
Three times: before, between and after the tasks

explanation: Handlers run once at the end of the play however many tasks notify them, which avoids repeated restarts.

stem: In a blue-green deployment, what do the two colours represent?

options.text: Two branches of the same Git repository
Two identical environments, one live and one idle
Two teams that must approve every release
Two databases that are kept in sync by hand every night

explanation: One environment serves users while the new version is prepared on the other, then traffic is switched.

stem: In GitOps, what is the source of truth for the desired state?

options.text: The objects currently running in the cluster
A runbook page in the team wiki
A Git repository holding the manifests
The log output from the last CI build

explanation: GitOps keeps desired state in Git and uses a controller to make the cluster match it.

stem: A canary release sends 5% of traffic to the new version. What is the main benefit?

options.text: The new version is tested without any real traffic at all
Both versions can share one database schema without any changes being made
Rollouts finish faster than with any other strategy
A bad release affects only a small share of users before wider rollout

explanation: Limiting exposure lets you watch metrics on real traffic and stop before most users are affected.

stem: Which approach makes rollback fastest in a blue-green deployment?

options.text: Switch the router back to the still-running previous environment
Rebuild the previous version from source code and deploy it again later
Restore the database from last night's backup first
Run the pipeline again with the earlier commit message

explanation: The old environment is still running, so rollback is a routing change instead of a rebuild.

stem: With self-heal enabled, a GitOps controller finds a Deployment edited by hand in the cluster. What does it do?

options.text: Copies the manual edit back into the Git repository
Reverts the cluster object to match the manifest in Git
Deletes the Deployment and waits for a manual approval before recreating it
Ignores the drift until the next scheduled release

explanation: The controller treats Git as truth and removes drift, so lasting changes must be made through Git.

stem: A release includes dropping a database column. Why does this make rollback risky?

options.text: Databases cannot be changed by deployment pipelines at all
Rollbacks always require a full restart of the database server
The old code may need the dropped column, so schema changes should be backward compatible
The column drop is automatically reversed when the pipeline fails

explanation: Rolling the app back does not bring the column back. Expand first, migrate, and contract in a later release.

stem: Which of these is a metric rather than a log line?

options.text: A stack trace printed when an exception is thrown
Requests per second over the last minute
A message saying a user signed in at 10:01
A debug line showing a SQL statement

explanation: Metrics are numbers measured over time and are cheap to aggregate. Logs are individual event records.

stem: Why ship logs from many servers to one central place?

options.text: To make each server's disk fill up faster
To stop applications from writing logs locally
To search and correlate them in one tool
To remove the need for any log retention rules

explanation: Debugging a request that crossed several servers needs all their logs searchable together.

stem: A service has a 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days. Roughly how much downtime does that allow?

options.text: About 7 hours
About 4 minutes in total
About 9 hours
About 43 minutes

explanation: 30 days is 43,200 minutes and 0.1% of that is about 43 minutes, which is the error budget.

stem: Why is average latency a poor single indicator of user experience?

options.text: A few very slow requests are hidden, so percentiles such as p95 or p99 matter
Average latency cannot be calculated from request data at all
Users only ever notice the fastest request in a session
Averages are always lower than the median value

explanation: Averages smooth over the slow tail that users actually feel. Percentiles show it.

stem: Which alerting approach is best practice?

options.text: Alert whenever any server's CPU passes 70% for a single second
Alert on symptoms users feel, such as an error rate above the SLO threshold
Alert on every warning line in the logs to be safe
Alert only when a customer opens a support ticket

explanation: Symptom-based alerts are actionable and cut noise. Cause-based alerts on every blip train people to ignore pages.

stem: Why log in a structured format such as JSON?

options.text: It makes log files smaller than any plain-text format could be
It removes the need to include a timestamp in each entry
Fields can be parsed, filtered and aggregated without fragile text matching
It stops logs from ever containing any sensitive data

explanation: Key-value fields let a pipeline query by user id or status code without regular expressions.

stem: What does a dependency scanner look for?

options.text: Syntax errors in your own source files
Known vulnerabilities in third-party libraries
Slow queries in the production database server's logs
Unused style rules in the front end

explanation: Scanners compare your dependency versions with databases of published vulnerabilities.

stem: Where should a CI pipeline get an API token from?

options.text: A constant defined in the application source code or its config file
A text file committed next to the pipeline file
The CI system's secret store, injected at run time
The title of the pull request that triggered it

explanation: Secret stores keep tokens out of the repository and can mask them in build logs.

stem: A deploy job only needs to push to one container registry. Which credential is best?

options.text: A personal token with access to every project
The cloud account's root user credentials
An admin token that is shared by all of the team's pipelines
A token scoped to push images to that one registry only

explanation: A narrow token limits what an attacker can do if the pipeline is compromised.

stem: A scan reports a critical vulnerability in a library you only use in tests. What is a sensible response?

options.text: Assess the exposure, then upgrade or record the risk with a deadline
Ignore it permanently because test code never reaches production at all
Delete the scanner so that it stops failing the build
Rewrite the library from scratch before shipping anything

explanation: Test-only code is lower risk but not zero (build agents hold secrets). Decide deliberately and track it.

stem: A secret was committed to Git and removed in the next commit. What should you do?

options.text: Nothing, since the latest commit no longer contains it in any file
Rotate the secret, because it remains in the Git history
Force-push the branch and keep using the same secret
Rename the file so scanners no longer match it

explanation: Anyone who cloned the repository can read old commits. Treat the secret as exposed and replace it.

stem: Which Kubernetes setting follows least privilege for a container?

options.text: Run as root so it can install packages whenever it needs
Mount the host's Docker socket for easier debugging
Run as a non-root user with a read-only root filesystem
Disable network policies so pods can talk to each other freely

explanation: A non-root user and read-only filesystem shrink what an attacker can do after breaking in.
